title: Impacts of Neighborhood Labels on Housing Demand
abstract: Expectations and sentiment of economic agents play a key role in the dynamics of housing markets. We study how neighborhood labels—designations that provide information about the quality of a neighborhood—affect housing demand. Using a regression discontinuity design around the boundaries of Qualified Opportunity Zones, we find that QOZ designations increase housing demand as measured by search activity and housing prices. The effects are concentrated in lower-income census tracts that are near the QOZ boundary, where the label provides novel positive information about neighborhood quality.

title: Air Pollution and Rent Prices: Evidence from Wildfire Smoke Plumes in Las Vegas
abstract: This paper leverages quasi-experimental wildfire smoke shocks to estimate the causal effect of air pollution on rent prices. Using data on wildfire smoke plumes in Las Vegas, Nevada and apartment-level rent data, we find that exposure to wildfire smoke plumes significantly reduces rent prices. The effects are driven by short-term pollution exposure and are concentrated in neighborhoods with lower income and lower housing quality, consistent with renters in those areas being less able to avoid polluted locations.

title: Gender Gaps in the Federal Reserve System
journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
abstract: To better understand the stalled progress of women in economics, we study gender gaps within the Federal Reserve System—the largest employer of economists in the United States. Using administrative data on all Federal Reserve economists from 2001 to 2021, we document significant gender gaps in hiring, pay, promotion, and attrition. Women are underrepresented at higher ranks, earn less than men conditional on rank and experience, are promoted more slowly, and leave the Fed at higher rates. These gaps are not explained by research productivity or field of specialization.

title: Adjusting to Macroprudential Policies: Loan-to-Value Limits and Housing Choice
abstract: Using a detailed loan-level dataset, this paper exploits a sharp policy change in Israel's loan-to-value (LTV) limits to identify how borrowers adjust their housing choices when access to credit is restricted. The findings show that constrained borrowers respond by purchasing smaller and cheaper homes in lower-quality neighborhoods rather than delaying homeownership. The results highlight that macroprudential policies have distributional consequences: tighter LTV limits primarily burden lower-income and younger borrowers who have fewer liquid assets to substitute for restricted borrowing.

title: More than Shelter: The Effect of Rental Eviction Moratoria on Household Well-Being
abstract: This paper investigates the impact of the 2020 COVID-19 rental eviction moratoria on household well-being. Using a regression discontinuity design around the expiration of local eviction moratoria and credit bureau data, we find that eviction moratoria significantly reduced financial distress, including delinquencies on credit cards, auto loans, and non-housing debt. The results suggest that housing stability prevents spillovers to broader financial distress, highlighting the importance of housing policy for household financial health beyond shelter provision.

title: The Effect of LTV-Based Risk Weights on House Prices: Evidence from an Israeli Macroprudential Policy
abstract: This paper examines the effect of an increase in capital requirements for high LTV mortgages on house prices in Israel. Using a regression discontinuity design around LTV thresholds that determine capital charges, we find that higher capital requirements reduce house prices in high-LTV segments of the market. The price effects are concentrated in areas with more credit-constrained households and greater dependence on mortgage financing, consistent with a demand channel through tighter credit supply.

title: Structural Changes in Israeli Family Farms: Long-Run Trends in the Farm Size Distribution and the Role of Part-Time Farming
abstract: This paper analyzes long-run structural changes in Israeli family farms using agricultural census data spanning several decades. We document a significant consolidation trend: the number of farms has declined sharply while average farm size has increased. Part-time farming has grown substantially and is shown to be an important mechanism enabling small farms to survive consolidation pressures. The findings are consistent with international evidence on farm size distribution dynamics and contribute to understanding the role of off-farm income in sustaining smallholder agriculture.

title: Macroprudential Policy: Implementation, Effects, and Lessons
abstract: The paper reviews the development of macroprudential policy in Israel from 2010 to 2018, focusing on the implementation of LTV limits and sectoral capital requirements targeting the housing market. It documents the policy measures taken, discusses the evidence on their effects on credit growth and house prices, and draws broader lessons for macroprudential policy design. The paper argues that coordinated and well-timed macroprudential tools can reduce systemic risk without severely constraining credit access.
